subject: english
topic: Reflect and Respond: literal and figurative phrases
prompt:
In the unit's opening activity, Anil and Sunny of the theatre club have had an argument. Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.

*Anil did not want to ______ and disturb Sunny further, but he finally decided to bite the bullet and speak to him.*

image.alt: One boy sulks under a rain cloud while his friend wonders what to say

options.text: throw a party
come around
bring it up
winding up

hint: Which phrase means 'to raise a topic for discussion'?
explanation: To **bring it up** means to raise a subject. Anil hesitates to mention the quarrel because it might upset Sunny more. The other phrases fit other blanks in the same paragraph: the club was **winding up** (finishing) its practice, Anil hoped Sunny would **come around** (become friendly again), and everyone asked them to **throw a party**. The book asks you to discuss which of these phrases are literal and which are **figurative**: 'bring it up' here is figurative, since nothing is physically lifted.

topic: Act I: why Shruti is distressed

She has forgotten the notes of the fusion piece
Her friends want her to leave the group

hint: What does Avinash guess when Shruti finally looks up?
explanation: Shruti has still not told her father about the **concert**. She fears he will think it a **desecration** (disrespect towards something sacred) of the violin to play it to Western tunes, since he believes Classical Hindustani music, with its **ragas and aalaaps**, is the only music worth playing. The newspaper actually **praised** her, and her friends want her to stay.

subject: english
prompt: At dinner, Nabin says *'No is the answer'* and reminds Shruti of his rule: one performance in every six months. Which reason does he give for this rule?

image.alt: A twelve-month calendar with two months marked with a violin

options.text: More performances would leave her no time for school work
Performing too often makes people value an artist less: familiarity breeds contempt
Concerts are too expensive for the family to attend
A violin needs six months of rest between concerts

hint: He uses a well-known proverb.
explanation: Nabin says that more than one performance in six months means **familiarity breeds contempt**: when people see something too often, they stop respecting it. (**Contempt** is a strong feeling of dislike and disrespect.) He advises her to 'work on your art and everything will follow'. School work, cost and resting the violin are never mentioned.

topic: Act II: drowning one's individual style
prompt: Nabin says it is not wise *'to drown your individual style in the hubbub of an orchestra'*. What is he worried about?

image.alt: A small violin beside a noisy jumble of loud instruments

options.text: Shruti might hurt her ears in a loud concert hall
Shruti would play so loudly that she spoils the orchestra
Shruti's own distinct style would be lost among the noise of many players
The orchestra would not allow Shruti to play the violin

hint: 'Hubbub' means a loud noise. What would be 'drowned' in it?
explanation: A **hubbub** is a loud noise. Nabin fears that in a **group performance**, Shruti's **individual style** would be swallowed up, so nobody would notice her own artistry. The phrase is **figurative**: nothing is literally drowned. He is not talking about her hearing, her volume or the orchestra's rules.

She pleads with him to attend one practice, he leaves mocking 'phoo' music, and Leela scolds her for hiding it.

prompt: Complete the summary of Act II: *Nabin was ______ in his decision and would not change his mind.* Tap the word from the box.

plea
clash

subject: english
prompt: Select the **three** statements that are true about **Act III**.

image.alt: Two hands clapping

options.text: Shruti planned to practise one last time and then tell her friends she could not join the performance
Nabin said Shruti had played a few notes of the raga incorrectly
Shruti's parents left the practice before it was over
Leela helped her husband see why he should support their daughter
Nabin admitted that he had underestimated the power of 'our own music'

hint: Think about Shruti's aside, Nabin's praise and his words to Shruti at the end.
explanation: In her **aside**, Shruti plans one last practice before dropping out. Her parents stay till the end, Nabin **claps furiously** and says she never lost sight of the notes of the raga, so the statements about wrong notes and leaving early are false. Nabin says **Leela opened his eyes**, and admits he **underestimated the power of our own music**: he feared fusion would take Shruti away from Indian music, but it did not.

subject: english
topic: Act III: who opened Nabin's eyes?
prompt: Nabin tells Shruti that someone else 'opened my eyes' and that she should thank that person. Tap that character.

image.alt: Two adults clap as four young musicians play, with numbered markers

explanation: Nabin says it was **Leela**, Shruti's mother, who **opened his eyes**: Nabin admits he 'had forgotten' his own past. Leela then tells Shruti how her father had once gone against his own family's wishes to play the violin. Her gentle humour and wisdom make her the **peacemaker** of the family.

subject: english
prompt: Tap the character who grew up in a **family of vocalists** but chose to play a Western instrument.

image.alt: Two adults clap as four young musicians play, with numbered markers

hint: Leela tells this story about her husband.
explanation: Leela reveals that Shruti's grandfather (**Nabin**'s father) and her uncles were all **vocalists** of a highly traditional school. Nabin chose the **violin**, a Western instrument, instead of training his voice. His story mirrors Shruti's: each wanted to try something new that a parent disapproved of, which is why he finally understands her.

subject: english
prompt: After the practice, Nabin exclaims, *'Wah, how soulful!'* What does he especially praise about Shruti's playing?

image.alt: A violin and a line of notes rising across a music staff

options.text: She played louder than everyone else in the group
She played a Western tune perfectly from memory
She sang along while playing the violin
She did not lose sight of the notes of the raga even once

hint: He is pleased that something from his own tradition was still there.
explanation: Nabin says Shruti **did not lose sight of the notes of the raga** even once and played it to excellence. This reassures him that fusion has not made her give up her classical roots. He even offers the group the **music room**, where they will have more equipment and can practise regularly.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Three singers on one side of a dashed line and a violin on the other

assertion: Nabin's father was pained when Nabin chose to play the violin.
reason: At that time the violin was not yet a part of classical Indian music, so his father saw the choice as a betrayal of family tradition.
hint: Leela explains why the choice hurt the family.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Leela says the family of vocalists had **painstakingly** (with great care and effort) kept their musical heritage alive. Because the violin was **not yet part of classical Indian music** then, Nabin's father saw his choice as a **betrayal** of family values. Nabin's present fear about fusion echoes his own father's fear long ago.

subject: english
topic: Vocabulary: worked his fingers to the bone
prompt: Leela says that Nabin *'worked his fingers to the bone'*. What does this mean?

image.alt: A young violinist practising late at night by lamplight

options.text: He worked extremely hard
He injured his fingers while practising
He played only very simple tunes
He gave up practising after a short time

hint: It is an idiom, not a description of an injury.
explanation: **To work one's fingers to the bone** is an **idiom** meaning to work very hard. Leela uses it to show that Nabin earned his success as a violinist through great effort, even without his family's support: 'see where the violin got him'. It is figurative, so it does not describe an injury.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A young violinist practising late at night by lamplight

assertion: Nabin came from a family of violinists, so playing the violin simply continued the family tradition.
reason: Nabin worked extremely hard to succeed as a violinist.
hint: Which instrument, or voice, did his father and uncles use?
explanation: A is false, R is true. Nabin's family were **vocalists**, not violinists; he went **against** their wishes when he took up the violin. R is true: Leela says he 'worked his fingers to the bone'. This is why his success as a master violinist and Principal of **Sangeetika Music School** was hard-won.

subject: english
topic: Critical Reflection: each bay, its own wind
prompt: Nabin finally says, *'After all each bay, its own wind.'* What does he mean?

image.alt: Two sailboats in two bays, each pushed by its own wind

options.text: Sailors must always check the weather before setting out
Every artist has a unique path and style of their own
Music sounds best when it is played near the sea
Children must always follow the path chosen by their parents

hint: The Speaking Activity says this line shows that one size does not fit all.
explanation: Just as each bay has its own wind, each person has a **unique journey and style**. The Speaking Activity notes that the line means a one-size-fits-all approach does not work for every person, and suggests stressing '**each**' and '**own**' in a thoughtful tone. Nabin accepts that Shruti's path can differ from his, the opposite of the idea that children must follow their parents' path.

subject: english
prompt: Nabin's change of mind about artistic freedom builds a bridge between ______.

image.alt: A bridge joins a sitar on one bank to a keyboard on the other

options.text: historical techniques and futuristic inventions
strict discipline and casual learning
traditional values and modern forms of expression
personal ambition and professional success

hint: Think of classical ragas on one side and Indo-Western fusion on the other.
explanation: Nabin stands for **traditional** Classical Hindustani music; Shruti's fusion group stands for **modern expression**. When he sees that she keeps the notes of the raga even within fusion, he accepts both, building a **bridge between tradition and modernity**. The play is not about inventions, casual learning or career success.

subject: english
prompt: At the end, Shruti hugs both her parents. Which word does **not** describe what this hug shows?

image.alt: A girl hugs her mother and father

options.text: reconciliation
acceptance
understanding
duty

hint: Is the hug an obligation, or a natural expression of feeling?
explanation: The hug shows **reconciliation** (making peace after the disagreement), **acceptance** of Shruti's choice, **understanding** between generations and **harmony** in the family. It is a spontaneous expression of love and gratitude, not something done out of **duty** (a task one is obliged to do).

subject: english
prompt: Which of these best explains the title **'Twin Melodies'**?

image.alt: Two coloured melody lines weave in and out of each other

options.text: Two kinds of music, and two generations, learn to exist together in harmony
Shruti has a twin sister who also plays the violin
The fusion group can play only two songs
Nabin and Shruti always play exactly the same tune together

hint: Think about Classical Hindustani music and Indo-Western fusion, and about Nabin's past and Shruti's present.
explanation: The 'twin melodies' are **traditional classical music** and **modern fusion**, which the play shows can coexist, as Shruti keeps the raga alive inside a fusion piece. The title also suggests two generations, father and daughter, whose journeys are alike: each broke away from a family tradition. Shruti has no twin, and the group's songs are never counted.

All three friends happily celebrate the newspaper review.

Leela tells Shruti about her father's own struggle
The friends rehearse a fusion piece in Iqbal's room

Iqbal reads out the newspaper's praise of Shruti

prompt: Tap the stage direction which shows that a character is speaking her private thoughts to the audience, while the other characters on stage cannot hear her.

image.alt: A page from a play script, with numbered markers

hint: Shruti uses this device in Act III, when she plans to practise one last time.
explanation: An **aside** is a dramatic device in which a character speaks directly to the audience; the other characters on stage are understood to be unaware of it. It lets the audience know what a character **thinks or feels**. In Act III, Shruti's aside reveals that she means to quit the group after one last practice. '(very loudly)' only tells the actor how to speak.

subject: english
topic: Writing a play script: the ellipsis
prompt: In the last line, Shruti hesitates. Tap the punctuation mark that a script-writer uses to show a **short pause or silence**.

image.alt: A page from a play script, with numbered markers

hint: It is three dots in a row.
explanation: An **ellipsis (…)** shows a short pause or silence for dramatic effect, as in Shruti's 'Yes, actually I … er … was finding the right words'. The **Writing Task** tips also say: put a colon after the speaker's name, use brackets to tell the actor how to deliver the words, include an aside where needed, and use non-lexical fillers such as 'er'.

subject: english
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A page from a play script

assertion: In a play script, the words written inside brackets are not spoken aloud by the actors.
reason: In a play script, a colon is placed after the speaker's name to introduce the words of the speaker.
hint: Both statements are correct rules. Does the colon rule explain why bracketed words are silent?
explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. Words in **brackets** are not spoken because they are **instructions** to the actor about how to deliver a line, such as (calmly but firmly), much as a reporting verb like 'he shouted' does in a story. The **colon** rule is a separate convention, and together with the speaker's name it is why a script needs no inverted commas.

subject: english
prompt: **Non-lexical fillers** are sounds such as 'uh' or 'um' that fill pauses in speech. Match each face with the filler it is most likely to say. One filler is not needed.

image.alt: A cartoon face
A cartoon face
A cartoon face
A cartoon face

right.text: whew
arrgh
hmmm
ahem-ahem
err

hint: Which sound do you make when a worry is over? When you are annoyed? When you clear your throat?
explanation: **Whew** shows relief (Face 1 breathes out with a sweat drop). **Arrgh** shows frustration (Face 2 grits its teeth). **Hmmm** shows thinking (Face 3 rests a hand on its chin). **Ahem-ahem** is a throat-clearing cough to get attention (Face 4), as Iqbal does before reading the newspaper. **Err** shows hesitation, like Shruti's 'I … er …' at dinner.

subject: english
prompt: Match each music word with its meaning. One meaning is not needed.

image.alt: Notes on a music staff above a widening wedge mark

right.text: the pattern of beats or time intervals in music
the speed or pace at which a piece of music is played
a mixture of loud, unpleasant sounds
how high or low a sound is
a series of musical notes moving upwards or downwards
a male voice that falls between the higher and lower ranges

hint: The spare meaning describes a 'baritone'.
explanation: **Rhythm** is the pattern of beats; **tempo** is the speed; **cacophony** is a jumble of harsh sounds (the opposite of melody); **pitch** is how high or low a sound is; a **scale** is a series of notes going up or down. The leftover meaning is **baritone**. The book also defines **bass** as the lowest tone or part in music and a **note** as a single sound at a certain pitch.

subject: english
prompt: The play opens with a fusion piece 'in its **crescendo**'. Each picture shows how the loudness of a piece of music changes from left to right. Which one shows a crescendo?

options.text: Wave P

image.alt: A sound wave

options.text: Wave Q

image.alt: A sound wave

options.text: Wave R

image.alt: A sound wave

options.text: Wave S

image.alt: A sound wave

hint: A crescendo 'gets louder and louder'.
explanation: A **crescendo** is a gradual increase in the volume or intensity of sound, so its wave grows taller and taller, as in **Wave R**. Wave P does the opposite and fades away. Wave Q stays at the same loudness, and Wave S jumps up and down without any steady build-up. In music, a widening wedge mark under the notes tells players to make a crescendo.

subject: english
prompt: Shruti tells her mother that if she is not allowed to take part, *'all our practice will go down the drain.'* What does **go down the drain** mean?

image.alt: A girl with a worried look thinks about two kinds of music

options.text: be praised by everyone
be wasted
be recorded
be repeated

hint: Think of water disappearing down a drain.
explanation: To **go down the drain** is to be **wasted**, like water lost down a drain. Without its violinist, the group cannot perform, so all its hard work would be for nothing. The other phrases in the same exercise are **drown your individual style** (lose what makes you unique) and **sense of musicality** (a natural feel for music).

subject: english
prompt: Lines such as *'Wah, how soulful!'* are **exclamatory sentences**. Which **two** steps does the book suggest for putting them into reported speech?

image.alt: An exclamation in a speech bubble turns into a sentence written in a notebook

options.text: Use 'exclaimed' or 'exclaimed with (a feeling)' instead of the reporting verb 'said'
Keep the interjection 'Wah' at the start of the reported sentence
Remove interjections, the exclamation mark and the quotation marks
End the reported sentence with a question mark
Keep the speaker's exact words inside inverted commas

hint: A reported sentence becomes an ordinary statement (a declarative sentence).
explanation: An **exclamatory** sentence expresses strong feeling. To report it, replace 'said' with **exclaimed** or **exclaimed with (joy, wonder…)**, and remove the **interjection**, the **exclamation mark** and the **quotation marks**, so it becomes a **declarative** sentence: *Nabin exclaimed with delight that the music was very soulful.* A question mark belongs only to questions, and inverted commas only to direct speech.

subject: english
prompt:
*“What an incredible achievement! I can't believe we pulled it off!” said Iqbal.*

Choose the correct reported form.

image.alt: Two friends cheer beside a trophy as confetti falls

options.text: Iqbal exclaimed that it is an incredible achievement and he can't believe we pulled it off.
Iqbal said that what an incredible achievement! He could not believe they had pulled it off.
Iqbal exclaimed that it was an incredible achievement and that he could not believe they had pulled it off.
Iqbal exclaimed that it was an incredible achievement and that I could not believe we had pulled it off.

hint: Check three things: the reporting verb, the tenses and the pronouns.
explanation: The correct version uses **exclaimed**, shifts tenses back (*is → was, can't → could not, pulled → had pulled*) and changes pronouns (*I → he, we → they*). Keeping present tenses and 'we' is wrong; so is keeping the exclamatory form 'what an … !', which cannot follow 'that'; and so is leaving 'I' and 'we' unchanged.

subject: english
prompt:
*Asma: “I accidentally spilled paint all over my canvas.”*

Which is the correct reported form?

image.alt: A canvas with a bright paint splash on an easel and a tipped paint pot

options.text: Asma said that she had accidentally spilled paint all over her canvas.
Asma said that I had accidentally spilled paint all over my canvas.
Asma said that she has accidentally spilled paint all over my canvas.
Asma said that she accidentally spills paint all over her canvas.

hint: The simple past moves one step back, and 'I' and 'my' must refer to Asma.
explanation: With a past reporting verb (**said**), the simple past *spilled* becomes the **past perfect** *had spilled*, and the pronouns change: *I → she, my → her*. Keeping 'I' or 'my', using the present perfect *has spilled*, or switching to the present tense *spills* are all errors.

subject: english
prompt: Asma said: *“Wow! What a unique experience I had at the art studio today!”* The word cards show the reported version. Tap the card that replaces the word **today**.

image.alt: A reported sentence split into word cards, with numbered markers

hint: Words of time and place change in reported speech: now → then, here → there.
explanation: In reported speech, **today** becomes **that day** (just as *tomorrow → the next day* and *now → then*). The other cards show other changes: *Wow!* is replaced by **exclaimed excitedly**, *I* becomes **she**, and the simple past *had* becomes the past perfect **had had**.

subject: english
prompt:
*“I don't want papa to feel that I don't care about his opinions, because I do.”*

Which words should Shruti **stress** to bring out the contrast in her feelings?

image.alt: A girl speaks while a bar meter shows loud and soft beats

options.text: 'papa' and 'opinions'
'don't' in the first part and 'do' in the second part
'want' and 'feel'
'care' and 'because'

hint: Which pair of words means opposite things?
explanation: Stressing **don't** and **do** highlights the **contrast** in Shruti's inner conflict: she does care about her father's opinions. The Speaking Activity suggests starting in a slightly lower tone to show concern and rising towards the end to show her **sincerity**. The other pairs carry no contrast.

children in Paraguay playing instruments made from scrap collected from landfills

a water nymph said to live in a river, spring or waterfall

explanation: **Raga Chikitsa** describes the healing power of music, and **Sangita Sudha** (seventeenth century) its effects on emotions. The **Recycled Orchestra of Cateura**, formed in Paraguay in **2012**, uses instruments made from landfill scrap. prompt: In *A Friend Found in Music* by Bryanna T. Perkins, the first four lines end with the words **ocean, shore, rhythm, core**. What is the rhyme scheme of these lines?

image.alt: Waves with music notes roll towards a girl standing on the shore

options.text: aabb
abab
abcb
abba

hint: Do 'ocean' and 'rhythm' rhyme with each other?
explanation: 'Shore' and 'core' rhyme, but 'ocean' and 'rhythm' do not rhyme with anything, so the pattern is **abcb**: only the second and fourth lines rhyme. The poem keeps this pattern (*blue/through*, *there/care*). This light, regular rhyme gives the poem a gentle, song-like **musical** quality, fitting its subject.

subject: english
prompt:
*Music is the needed friend*
*When no one seems to care.*

The poet uses a **metaphor** here. Which sentence turns it into a **simile**?

image.alt: A smiling music note holds hands with a girl

options.text: Music is like a needed friend when no one seems to care.
Music is the friend I need when no one seems to care.
My friend needs music when no one seems to care.
Music, my needed friend, is there when no one seems to care.

hint: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
explanation: A **metaphor** says one thing *is* another (*Music is the needed friend*). A **simile** compares them using **like** or **as**: *Music is like a needed friend*. The other options are still metaphors or change the meaning. The poem's other metaphors call music an **ocean**, a **rhythm** and a **therapy**.

subject: english
prompt:
*Music is the therapy*
*I need when I feel blue.*

What does the phrase **feel blue** mean here?

image.alt: A girl in blue listens to music on headphones

options.text: feel cold
feel calm and peaceful
feel jealous
feel sad or low

hint: The poet needs 'therapy' at that moment.
explanation: **To feel blue** is an idiom meaning to feel **sad or low**, a **negative** emotion. Music is the **therapy** that heals this sadness. By contrast, **lifts my spirits** and **most cheerful** express positive emotions. The phrase is figurative: it has nothing to do with colour or temperature.

subject: english
prompt: Which word best describes the **mood** of the poem *A Friend Found in Music*?

image.alt: An open poetry book with a pencil and floating music notes

options.text: nostalgic
thoughtful
amused
playful

hint: The poet calmly reflects on what music means to her.
explanation: The poem is **thoughtful**: the poet reflects on how music comforts her, lifts her spirits and stays with her like a friend. It is not **nostalgic**, as she is not longing for the past, and it is neither **amused** nor **playful**, as it contains no humour or games. The repeated 'I', 'me' and 'my' show that the speaker is the poet herself.

prompt: Select the **three** lines in which the poet uses a **metaphor** that calls music something else.

image.alt: A magnifying glass moves over the lines of a poem

options.text: Music is the ocean
It's clear, music was there.
Music is the therapy
The times when I'm most cheerful,
Music is the needed friend

hint: Look for 'Music is the …' followed by something music is compared to.
explanation: In a **metaphor**, one thing is said to *be* another. The poet calls music an **ocean** that pulls her to the shore, a **therapy** for sadness and a **needed friend** when nobody cares. 'Music was there' simply says music was present, and 'the times when I'm most cheerful' describes a feeling; neither compares music to anything.

prompt: Arrange these phrases in the order in which they appear in the poem.

items.text: Music lifts my spirits
Music is the ocean
Music is the needed friend
Music is the therapy
Music is the rhythm

hint: The poem begins with the sea and ends with a friend.
explanation: The poem moves from the **ocean** that pulls the poet to the shore, to the **rhythm** that moves her to the core, to the **therapy** she needs when she feels blue, to music that **lifts her spirits** so she can pull through, and ends with music as the **needed friend** when no one seems to care.

prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: The same music note repeated in a row with echo rings

assertion: Many lines of the poem begin with the word 'Music'.
reason: Repeating the word keeps the reader's attention on how central music is to the poet's life.
hint: Why would a poet keep returning to the same word?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Five lines begin with **Music**, a use of **repetition**. Each time, music is given a new role (ocean, rhythm, therapy, friend), so the repetition **emphasises** that music is at the centre of her life. It also gives the poem a steady, song-like beat.

prompt: **Phrasal verbs** join a verb with a preposition or adverb to make a new meaning, as in *pull through*. Match each phrasal verb with its meaning. One meaning is not needed.

image.alt: A house, packed boxes and a small van driving away

right.text: to leave a place where one has been living
to begin living in a new home or place
to start doing or discussing something new
to start moving; to leave
to succeed in doing something very difficult
to shift position to make space for someone or something

hint: The spare meaning belongs to 'move over', as in 'Move over so I can sit down'.
explanation: You **move out** of an old home and **move in** to a new one. After a long time in a job, it is time to **move on**. A bus **moves off** once passengers are seated. In the poem, music helps the poet **pull through**, that is, succeed in getting through hard times, although 'pull' and 'through' alone mean something quite different. The extra meaning is **move over**.

topic: Writing: format of an invitation letter
prompt: You are inviting your grandparents to your school's musical evening on **World Music Day, 21 June**. You will give a sitar performance there. Arrange the parts of the letter in the correct order.

image.alt: An invitation card rising out of an envelope

items.text: Body: ask about their well-being, give the event details and request them to come
Date
Name of the sender
Sender's address
Complimentary close: Yours affectionately,
Salutation: Dear …

hint: The letter starts with where it comes from and when it was written, and ends with who wrote it.
explanation: The format given in the book is: **sender's address**, **date**, **salutation** (Dear …), **body** (well-being, event details with date, time and venue, and the request to attend), **complimentary close** (*Yours affectionately,*) and the **name of the sender**. Because the letter goes to grandparents, it is written in a **warm, personalised** style using 'I', 'we' and 'you'.

subject: english
prompt: In your letter inviting your grandparents to the musical evening, tap the part where you would give the **date, time and venue** of the event.

image.alt: The layout of a letter with numbered markers

hint: The date at the top tells when the letter was written, not when the event is.
explanation: The **body** of the letter carries the message: after asking about your grandparents' well-being, you give the details of the event (the musical evening on **21 June**, its time and venue) and request them to attend. The date at the top is only the **date of writing**. The salutation greets them, and *Yours affectionately,* closes the letter.
